thread.title: Umatilla County Fair Court ready to celebrate county's bounty
thread.title_full: Umatilla County Fair Court ready to celebrate county's bounty

author: Berit Thorson | East Oregonian
title: Umatilla County Fair Court ready to celebrate county's bounty
text:
UMATILLA COUNTY — Two young ladies from opposite ends of Umatilla County are representing the best of the county as the Fair Court this year.
Princesses Dena Loiland and Morgan Harris bring a depth of experience with local chapters of the National FFA Organization to their new roles. Beth Wheeler, the county fair coordinator and court chaperone, said it was important to the court’s selection committee to find princesses who felt ready to represent the whole county, beyond just themselves.
“We’re trying to make sure they know who and what they’re representing,” she said. “Not just the fair, but the county as a whole.”
The court will be present throughout the Umatilla County Fair. They can be seen helping in the barns each morning as well as at the Les Schwab stage during some events.
Loiland and Harris will be signing autographs inside the exhibitor hall Wednesday, Aug. 12, 3-4 p.m., Friday, Aug. 14, 2-3 p.m.; and Saturday, Aug. 15, 3-4 p.m.
On Friday evening, Aug. 14, the fair court and visiting royalty will host a meet-and-greet outside the concert gate 7:30-8:30 p.m. ahead of the Eli Young Band performance, which starts at 9 p.m.
Meet the princesses Loiland, taking after her sister as a fair princess, is a recent graduate of Weston-McEwan High School in Athena. She has participated as an exhibitor at fairs since 2018, and in 2024-25, Loiland earned the Overall Reserve Grand Champion Market Goat at the county fair. She also has been named the Oregon State Fair Public Speaking Champion and represented Oregon on the 2025 National 4-H Quiz Bowl and Skillathon teams.
She plans to study animal science in college with the goal of becoming a veterinarian. Loiland said she’s excited to offer the same encouragement to other young people that she’s received over the years.
Wheeler, the coordinator, said she appreciated Loiland’s background in public speaking and was excited to have a princess from the county’s eastern side.
“Dena is a phenomenal speaker,” she said of Loiland’s interview for the role. “I really enjoyed that she could present herself so well.”
Loiland’s counterpart on the court, Harris, just finished her freshman year at Echo High School. She’s been part of 4-H since she was 5 years old, eventually showing market steers as well as dairy heifers and static exhibits. Harris earned first place in dairy judging at the Umatilla County Fair in 2024, and sent three food items to the Oregon State Fair.
Harris is a three-sport athlete, playing volleyball, basketball and softball. She also serves as a volunteer firefighter with the Echo Rural Fire Protection District, with which she’s earning her CPR certification.
Eventually, Harris hopes to study veterinary science or agricultural business before returning home to work on her family’s farm. She said she’s excited to improve her public speaking as well as see the year-round work required to host the fair.
Wheeler said Harris’s personality drew the selection committee to her during the interview.
“Morgan just shined in all aspects of her conversation,” Wheeler said. “She’s genuine when she talks, she’s well-known in our county and she had aspirations of seeing what our county was more about than just her immediate surroundings.”
Princesses prepare for public-facing roles Becoming a Umatilla County Fair Court princess requires completing an application as well as participating in an interview with a selection panel. Wheeler said the panel selecting this year’s court included people from Pendleton and Hermiston, herself, a past princess and a community business representative.
“Everything’s done on the same point system so that it’s fair across the board,” she said.
Once selected, the princesses participate in a regional weekend clinic called “Now You Have the Crown,” during which they learn the ins and outs of being a court member. They attend sessions focused on hair and makeup, hat care, public speaking, the basics of rodeos and how the Pro Rodeo Cowboy Association Columbia River Circuit works. The circuit includes the Farm-City Pro Rodeo in Hermiston, which takes place the same days as the fair, Aug. 12-15.
Wheeler added that Loiland and Harris seemed to be good to pair together.
“I think that both of them being outgoing, they could glean from one another,” she said, “and push each other and help each other grow.”
The search has already begun for the court’s successors, with 2026-27 applications opening July 13. Wheeler said she hopes shifting the application process earlier — so it coincides with when the princesses are most in the public eye — will increase interest in the role among ladies across the county.
“Most courts complete their reign after their own specific event, but what’s right after our county fair is another traditional county event,” Wheeler said. “I feel it’s important for those fair court participants to be part of that other county tradition and we should be showing the same support that we are asking of others for us.”
Starting this year, princesses will serve Oct. 1 through Sept. 30, rather than in line with the calendar year. That way, the court will end its reign with Pendleton Round-Up events before passing the sashes to other young community leaders.
summary: Princesses Dena Loiland and Morgan Harris bring a depth of experience with local chapters of the National FFA Organization to their new roles.
